brief.topic: Myth: a prompt tweak is a small change
brief.audience: PMs and engineers who edit production prompts
constraints: Example is illustrative and labelled on screen and in caption

coreInsight: A prompt edit changes behaviour across every case, not just the one you looked at, so version it, re-run the eval set and roll it out like a release.

hooks.text: That one-line prompt edit is a release.
hooks.notes: Short, surprising, and the reel backs it up.

hooks.text: Your prompt tweak broke something you didn’t test.
hooks.notes: Assumes a failure the viewer may not have.

hooks.text: Why “just tweak the prompt” goes wrong.

scenes.purpose: Show how a small prompt edit can fix one case and break another (illustrative).

scenes.purpose: The release routine for prompt changes.
scenes.onScreen: SHIP PROMPTS LIKE CODE / Before a prompt change ships: / Version it, with a note on why · Re-run the full eval set · Compare with the last version · Roll out to a slice; keep rollback / No eval run, no prompt change in production.
scenes.voiceover: Before a prompt change ships: version it, with a note on why. Re-run the full eval set. Compare with the last version. Roll out to a slice, and keep a rollback. No eval run, no prompt change in production.

caption.opening: “Just tweak the prompt” is how a fix for one complaint quietly breaks three other kinds of answer.
body: In the illustrative example, “keep answers short” fixed long answers and also cut safety steps from how-to answers.

Before a prompt change ships:
→ Version it, with a note on why
→ Re-run the full eval set
→ Compare with the last version
→ Roll out to a slice and keep a rollback

claims.text: Prompt changes can affect behaviour beyond the case they target, so they should be versioned, evaluated against the full eval set and rolled out gradually.
Example: adding 'keep answers short' fixed long answers but removed safety steps from how-to answers.
